utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis this morning, for the time being. Judge Stole had a personal problem to attend to. He will be with us later on, hopefully. Madam Registrar, that being the case, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. The Prosecution today is represented by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye and Ms. Soljan. Amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic, Ms. Nikolic, Mr. Josse and Mr. Haynes. All right. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were the organs in charge of civilian affairs within the corps supposed to keep a record of humanitarian aid going to territories under Muslim control, including the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was their duty to record what passes through the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D836. This is an order from the Main Staff or, rather, a notification from the Main Staff, dated 22nd of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the very bottom of page 1, we see the following. Could we have the bottom of page 1 in B/C/S, please. In that very last paragraph, we see that the Command of the Drina Corps must urgently gather, arrange and submit the overview of humanitarian aid delivered to Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde for the month of July, July 1994. I'm interested in what we can find at page 2 of this document, page 2 in the B/C/S version and in the English version. In the very last sentence, we read that when building material comes in, the Main Staff has to be informed immediately by calling phone number 249. Why was building material of such importance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The construction material was important because it could have been used besides its basic main purpose for building fortifications which could have been used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D907. This is a notification from the Main Staff, dated 28th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, we see that two tons of cement have to go through for Srebrenica. This is related to a Swedish project. Do you remember that Swedish project?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In 1995, was that Swedish project --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Fauveau repeat her question? The interpreter has not understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame, they have a problem. If you could repeat your question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the Swedish project continued in 1995 and if material, aid and various equipment were delivered to Srebrenica as part of this project?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the materials were given for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please wait until the English translation is over before she begins her question in French. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, the interpreters are having a problem, and this is mainly caused by you jumping straight in to answer the question before they have finished translating. If you could allow for a short interval, please, before you start your answer. That's number 1. The other thing, the same applies to you, Madame Fauveau. You're doing exactly the same, and if you could please make the adjustment accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This document is dated 28th of May, 1995. We all know that on the 25th of May, NATO planes bombed Republika Srpska. During that period and immediately after the bombing, were convoys still passing? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the air bombardment, the convoys were stopped for a period of time, without announcement to the Main Staff of the reasons why they were suspended.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who took the decision to suspend the convoys during that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that this was a decision by the UNPROFOR Command. The information was based on the information from the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the army of Republika Srpska and the Main Staff receive information with respect to the use of humanitarian aid delivered to the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska had reliability information that a part of the humanitarian aid was being delivered to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was in the enclaves, and this was done through some separate channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1360.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a document coming from the Ministry of Defence from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and from the department of that ministry in Srebrenica. This is sent to the Tuzla department, and here we have a list of the quantities of food and fuel that were delivered to military formations or units that were located on the Srebrenica territory in 1995, in March 1995. We see that there was 18 tons of flour, 6 tons of beans, and so on and so forth. Could you have a look at the last paragraph: [In English] "... that the above quantities were allotted from a consignment of humanitarian which arrived in this area through the UNHCR, and this is the only source of supply." [Interpretation] You stated that you had information related to the use of humanitarian aid by the army. Were you aware that such quantities were involved?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have precise information. I had information about the kind of article we are talking about, but the authorised services had some adequate quantities or commensurate quantities for their sources. We knew that that was the way to supply them, through the UNHCR, so this is why we stepped up our checks, and also with the appropriate restrictions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D955. This is a similar document, but a document that relates to the month of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We see that the military units at Srebrenica received 25 tons of flour, sugar as well. And in the third paragraph: [In English] "We wish to note that the above quantities have been separated out of the humanitarian aid contingent which arrived in the area through UNHCR, while some of the food was obtained from the Dutch Battalion." [Interpretation] You stated that you had information related to the UNHCR. Were you aware of the fact that the Dutch-Bat, which was in Srebrenica, were you aware that the Dutch-Bat provided food to the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, that information was known to the Main Staff. The quantities were not disclosed to the section, and that is why controls were stepped up and a planned supplying was required for. And on the basis of that planned supply, the estimates were made as to how much exactly that battalion required. And then from the quantity that they received, they would set aside one part for the needs of the B and H army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that within the corps, a record was kept of the quantities of cargo that was going through. I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D952. This is a list of goods delivered to the enclaves in Eastern Bosnia in April 1994. We see, for example, that in Srebrenica, in April 1994, 229 tons of flour were delivered. I know that at the time you were not at the Main Staff. You arrived at the Main Staff in November. But at the beginning of 1995, did you notice a change in the quantity of goods authorised by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff's policy was to let through to the enclaves as much material and as many articles as were really needed, because it was geared to supply the units that were in the protected areas; and the focus was on materials that could be used for military purposes, like building materials, tinned food, and different other supplies. I'm not able to give you the precise information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D953. Here we have the quantities of goods delivered to the enclaves in March and April 1995. This is a document coming from the Command of the Drina Corps. In the first four columns, we are dealing with March, and the next columns relate to April. I'm not going to go into a detailed analysis of this document. I think the figures speak for themselves. We have the figures for flour for Srebrenica in March and April.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The only question I have about this document is whether there was a change in the policy related to authorisations delivered by the Main Staff or by the coordination body was changed. I think my question has not properly been translated. Was such a change noticed in March 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was the same. Nothing was changed unless there was some particular intelligence data that any specific material was expected and its possible use of -- and its possible use for military purposes. As for the procedures, the policy was the same, and that was that humanitarian convoys had to be allowed to go through and checked in the way that they were checked up until then, and allowed unimpeded access.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Ms. Fauveau. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye. Shall we make an effort to finish with this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll do my best to finish with him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please. Otherwise, we will make you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my colleagues, and good morning to you, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My name is Kweku Vanderpuye, and on behalf of the Prosecution, I'm going to put some questions to you in relation to your direct examination by my colleague. If I ask you any questions that are unclear to you, please let me know, and I'll do my best to try and rephrase it or ask it in a way that we can better understand one another. Now, you first arrived at the Main Staff in the beginning of 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that I arrived in late 1994, on the 3rd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you remained working at the Main Staff throughout July 1995, at least; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, of course, you know the accused in this case General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know General Miletic, and I am aware of the fact that he's accused here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you know that he's charged with very serious crimes before this Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, the entire indictment is not clear to me, except for the part that relates to the humanitarian function.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I just want to know if understand whether or not he's charged with serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that he's accused of serious crimes. In my reparation for the testimony, I focused only on humanitarian aid, what was in the domain of the work of our section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. From your knowledge, do you know what he is accused of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know, from newspapers, radio, television, what was available to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what was available to the public that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That he's charged for violating the conventions of war and the customs of war, and preventing humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's enough. Let's move forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also know General Gvero; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you know both Generals Gvero and Miletic in your professional capacity, as you worked with them in 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know either of them on a personal level as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know them outside of your professional association with them during 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your duties in 1995, it's fair to say that you spoke to both of them on numerous occasions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you corresponded with them as well on numerous occasions; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the same goes for General Tolimir as well; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you worked for the sector for relations with international organisations or foreign forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And your immediate supervisor, you said, was Milos Djurdjic. He was the chief; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And he reported directly, I think you said, to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time. Later on, to General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us a little bit about your unit? Tell us, for example, who worked in connection with foreign relations or relations with international organisations at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Receiving information, and all contacts went through our office. And when they requested that a meeting be held, meetings were held with UNPROFOR at the level of the appropriate chain of command, which means that the commander of the Main Staff met with the UNPROFOR commander; the Chief of Staff of the army of Republika Srpska met with the UNPROFOR Chief of Staff. Colonel Djordjevic [as interpreted], at his level, met with the coordination body or the UNPROFOR office at Pale. I was in contact with them if somebody called on the phone and spoke English, and then I would relay the instructions as to what needed to be done, or I would forward that call to the appropriate person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned -- or it reads in the transcript, just so we know, you mentioned Colonel Djordjevic, or that's how it reads. Is that correct, or is it actually Colonel Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic. It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about Radislav Pandzic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know Colonel Radoslav Pandzic at the time, and we were often in contact on the topic of the over-flights of helicopters over the protected area, and controlling the helicopters, which was done at the sports grounds in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, obviously, based on your direct testimony, General Mladic had to do with dealings with UNPROFOR, as did General Milovanovic, Tolimir, and General Miletic. Can you tell us who else was involved in dealings with UNPROFOR or international organisations in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some commissions, such as the Commission for Frequencies, and this commission involved Colonel Babic. Later on, there was the mine removal commission, de-mining mission, but that was at a lower point. At one point, as regards road maintenance, the chief of engineers was in contact with UNPROFOR on that issue, Mihajlo Djurdjevic; he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that it, as far as your recollection is concerned in -- well let's say between January and July of 1995, in terms of dealing with UNPROFOR or UNPROFOR related matters in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's as much as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think you said yesterday when you transferred from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff, initially you were utilised as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only at the beginning, but throughout my tenure in the Main Staff, I was primarily an interpreter, and working with humanitarian organisations was a sideline, as were other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you took on additional activities during 1995, and you said at page 29256 of the transcript that you became familiar with all of the procedures relating to the cooperation with UNPROFOR and other international organisations. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as part of your function, you assisted Colonel Djordjevic [sic] you prepared -- I'm sorry, Djurdjic, and you prepared required documents in his absence that were related to convoy requests; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What kind of documents are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were requests filed by UNPROFOR to allow passage through VRS-controlled territory. The documents would come from their office at Pale to the office of Colonel Djurdjic. The documents would then be examined. The Serb and the English versions of the text would be collated, and any errors that may have been caused by bad communications would be rectified, or in some cases the text was illegible, and then the documents were submitted for the information and approval of either General Mladic or General Milovanovic. And once they gave their approval or made some remarks, the documents were further processed in the typing pool. That was under my control. And then the documents were again taken to General Milovanovic - that was the regular procedure - for his signature. And then they went back to -- they were sent back to the UNPROFOR office, using our communications equipment, to the corps that actually had to take action; in other words, carry out the checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I thank you for that explanation in procedure, and I apologise if my question was a bit inartful. When I said what documents were you talking about, I was referring to the documents you prepared, because that's what you stated in line 10 at page 29256 of your testimony yesterday. So when you say you prepared documents, can you tell us what specific documents you prepared?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we dealt with those requests, as I have already described. That's number 1. Number 2, letters came in from the chief of the UNPROFOR Command and from the UNPROFOR Command. Sometimes they were in English, and sometimes they were in both languages, and then the two versions had to be compared, checked, and draft replies based on what Generals Mladic and Milovanovic had said, their comments. And then the reply would be taken back to the generals for their comments and approval, and then it was sent back to the UNPROFOR office. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And when you received these documents, and specifically I'm referring to requests, convoy request documents from UNPROFOR, you would eventually pass them up the chain of command; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in some cases, not only Colonel Djurdjic but you, yourself, made certain recommendations regarding the disposition of those requests; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We provided appropriate information, information that had been sought about some kinds and quantities of goods that had passed through; and we had documents signed by UNPROFOR and by representatives of the army of Republika Srpska as to what the procedure was and what had been agreed in those documents, and this is what we brought up, what we warned about. So we didn't make any proposals to limit anything or to deny permission for anything. We simply brought up the existing documents that had been signed by UNPROFOR and by appropriate representatives of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You've mentioned the term "we" on several occasions, and if you could, just tell us who you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to Colonel Djurdjic and myself, because we dealt exclusively with those requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you get these requests, you'd review them; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you'd look at each specific individual request that you received from UNPROFOR; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And before you passed it up the chain of command, you'd write down on the specific request "yes" or "no"; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, we did not write either "yes" or "no" on the requests. Those who approved the requests would put the "yes" or "no" in the upper right-hand corner. It would be written there either by General Mladic or General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 4001 in e-court, please. I do apologise to the Court. We don't have a particular translation for this document, but I think we can have the witness explain for sufficient purposes what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court what this document is, what type of a document it is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is a document that was sent on the 25th of February, 1995, to the UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo. On the basis of the requests sent by the UNPROFOR Command, we informed them that we have approved the passage of UNPROFOR convoys in the Republika Srpska territory as follows. And then the convoys are listed. Convoy number 26, 30802 from Kiseljak to Sarajevo and back. The date is the 26th of February, 1995. Then the convoy number 26, 316/02 from Kiseljak to Sarajevo and back. The date is the 26th of 1995 [as interpreted], and so on and so forth, and all the way down to item number 10 or, rather, 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kralj. If we could just page down so he can see the signature on this. Do you recognise that signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the signature of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go over to page 2 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you see some markings right in the center at the top of the page and to the left of where it says "UNPROFOR, Glavni Stab Sarajevo." There is a circle with the word "da" written in it, and then there is a symbol next to that. If you could tell us -- if we could just blow that up so everybody could see, that would be better. Yes, maybe a bit bigger. That would be good. Can you see that, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And whose initials are those to the right of that circle?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initials are those of General Ratko Mladic. It is also his handwriting. So "da" is written in his hand, and so is the circle around the word "da," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, if we could go over to -- well, let's go to the next page. Now, on this page you can see a circle and a symbol next to it, and the word "da" written in the circle. Do you see that, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as the previous document, this is the initials -- these are the initials of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 12. It should be ERN 7783. Okay. Here we see a circle with the word "da" in it next to a larger circle with the word "nee" in it, and it's crossed out with a question mark. And to the right of that, there is some writing. If that can be blown up so Mr. Kralj can see that, the writing part. Is that it? Thank you. Can you read what that says, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, somebody returned the document to me to check why "no" was written there. Somebody had already gone through the document, and apparently this was not General Mladic or General Milovanovic, because they would have put their initials and indicated "yes" or "no." So somebody had gone through this document, the document that I had not submitted for examination, but it was then returned to the office so I could see what this was all about. And after it was verified that everything was all right, the document went through the normal procedure and the word "da" was put there. I can't tell you who actually approved the document, because there are no initials here. There was no reason, however, to deny permission. So this word "no" was crossed out and a question mark was put there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who could have crossed it out and sent it back to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer if you know. I don't want you to speculate, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not what I meant. I didn't tell you, "Tell us if you know who sent it, and don't tell us anything if you don't know who sent it." The answer is this -- or, rather, the question was: Could you indicate a list of people who could have possibly sent you this? Who would they be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the duty manager or administrator, because he was superior to the duty officer who was in charge of gathering all the mail that had to be submitted to General -- that went up to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What does it say on this document to the right that's written with the question mark following it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Kralj, why not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you have no idea who would have sent that to you; by name, in particular?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because this document pertains to military observers and there is a rotation of interpreters, so this is not controversial at all. It was always approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me intervene a little bit here. Do you remember this document at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have 65 ter 4006, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, do you recognise this particular letter? We can zoom out a little bit so you can see the whole first page, but it might be a little easier for you to read the title and perhaps maybe the first paragraph to orient yourself to this document. Do you remember this document, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall the activities that are related to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could go I think to page 2. It should be ERN ending 8047.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is direct your attention, sir, to the handwritten portion on the bottom of this letter, and let us know if it's large enough for you to read it. Are you able to read that, sir, or should we make it bigger?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is large, but it's illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you can see at the very beginning it's directed to you. That's your name; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it addresses you as Lieutenant Kralj; right? Or Lieutenant-Colonel Kralj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we just started with this witness, could you please ask the witness if he remembers this document at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember this document, Mr. Kralj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before I remember the contents of the document, but I don't remember the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was processed by Colonel Djurdjic in cooperation with Colonel Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you've just stated a few seconds ago, namely, that you remember the contents of the document, but not the document itself, does that apply also to the previous document about which I asked you, whether you remembered it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This applies to this document. Documents like this one that affected the airspace or violations of airspace were something that we were regularly informed about, and these documents, after they went into the processing procedure, were archived also at our section. We monitored what was happening. So here what happened was that somebody ordered me to do this; and it was processed by Colonel Djurdjic, in cooperation with Colonel Pandzic, who was in charge of helicopter flights and those issues. Often, the document would be processed in a different organ, but because this was work with the UNPROFOR Command, the document was archived with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we zoom this up for the witness, he may be able to read it. Let's give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the handwritten piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the handwritten piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it can be zoomed a little bit further. To the right, yes. Yes. You have the original which you can show him. Probably it will be a little more legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Hopefully, the original is on its way. We don't have it just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says in the first sentence: "Lieutenant-Colonel Kralj, study this letter," meaning the letter has already been drafted and then is being given to me to review it. I didn't take part in the drafting of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I appreciate that, but you did study it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It says "give it back" or "return it," but then I cannot see it anymore. But I am familiar with the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you were directed to do that by Colonel Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what Colonel Djurdjic said. This is his remark at the bottom, for me to look over this letter. Probably he was planning to be absent for a period of time, so in case it was necessary, he wanted me to be informed about it. But this is the first time that I am seeing this type of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And on the bottom right -- the bottom right corner of this document, you can see Colonel Djurdjic's signature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is his signature, and that was his remark, for me to familiarise myself with this particular document as well as the procedure on how this kind of document is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And just for the record, the signature that is immediately below the name of Manojlo Milovanovic, that is General Milovanovic's signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Milovanovic's signature. You can see that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to clarify something with you, just so that I understand you clearly. It's your testimony that you never actually wrote anything on any of these request documents that were received from UNPROFOR; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be certain, but I didn't decide for anything to go out. I could have given some sort of remark or observation in terms of the regulations pertaining to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say you could have given a remark about that, do you mean that orally or do you mean that in a written sense, because my question is whether or not you wrote anything on these types of documents.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, the copy that is going to the archives indicated as A/A, unless this was indicated earlier. It was put on the archive document that that copy would be going to the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that's what you would write, "A/A," and nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But you did receive a fair number of these documents coming back your way; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's why you were able to recognise immediately the signature of General Mladic, the signature of General Tolimir, the signature of General Milovanovic, the signature of Radoslav Pandzic. You were able to recognise all those signatures because you were very familiar with the signatures on these documents that came back your way; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 4039 in e-court, please. All right, thank you very much. If we can jump two pages forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose signature that is, sir, that you see next to the circle where it says "da"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you're sure about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure that it's not Mladic and not Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you have no idea whose signature that is; is that what you're telling us, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature is questionable. I cannot really say whose it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look, please, at 65 ter 4028. All right, thank you for that. If we could just go one page forward, 65 ter ending -- I'm sorry, ERN ending 7146.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise -- it's just as well. Do you recognise the symbol that is depicted there on the right, where it is indicated "UNPROFOR"? It's on the right top side of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's General Mladic's initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Could I just see the top of this document, so I know which page I'm on. All right. We can go to page ending 7150. It should be two pages forward. Page 6, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, if I could just direct your attention to the handwritten portion, and immediately beneath the handwritten portion, you'll see a slash and a symbol. Can you tell us whose initials those are?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about these initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. These are the ones next to the slash beneath the writing. You're not sure what the initials are to the right of that slash; is that what you're saying, just so I'm clear?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could, could we have 5D1404 in e-court. Let's just go back to the other document. That was 65 ter 4028, and it was page 6 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us what the handwritten portion of this document says? And if you can't, let us know and my colleague will read it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to have this read to me. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, we'll to that. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "No, but this should be seen by Toso and Gvero. There is no need for the officer to be at the DK, but think about where he would be if to --" and I cannot read the last word and the initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Picking it up from Judge Kwon, do you think if we blew up the last part, you would be able to read it, Ms. Soljan? Let's blow it up, because otherwise you can't give us an answer. Yes. Does it help you better now? All right, let's see if the witness can manage instead. Yes, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am -- I am trying to read. If you can give me just a little bit more time. I cannot read it, but I can see that this is General Mladic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where do you see General Mladic's signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Underneath the last word in the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And beneath that, where the forward slash is, and you can see some writing, can you tell us whose signature that is or whose initials those are?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And let's go up the screen, if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the right of the screen, can you tell us whose initials those are?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see on this document that it is directed towards Toso, who you said yesterday was General Tolimir; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it was directed towards Gvero, who I think you said you knew as General Gvero; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document also has "A/A." I think that indicates it went to the archives. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, the document is from the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And as best as you can see, is this handwriting directed towards anybody besides Generals Tolimir and General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see here that it was sent to Toso and Gvero. This is legible, the first part of it, for their information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. If I could have a look at 65 ter 4036. All right, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, you can see this is from the Main Staff, and it's directed towards the UNPROFOR Command. And if we could go to -- all right. If we could just go down so you can see the bottom. Can you tell us whose signature that is at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whose signature this is, but obviously it is not the signature of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for that. If we could go -- I think it would be page 4 on e-court. It should be the ERN ending 6842. First, if we can go straight to the bottom and blow up the signature at the bottom of this page. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature at the very bottom of this page, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the signature of Lieutenant-Colonel Vlacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go to the top of this document, first I want to focus you, if I could, on the symbol next to the word "January" or "Januar," and it's just outside the circle. Can you tell us whose initials those are?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, where it says "yes," "da," that's General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, above that, you can see writing, just above the circle, and the writing says "Gvero and Toso"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says "Gvero and Toso."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And immediately above that, can you read what that says? And if you can't, let me know and my colleague will give it another try.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we blow this up a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Let them go to Kiseljak, and then from there by car." [In English] "Gvero and Toso," exclamation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As far as you can see, sir -- first of all, as far as you can see on the screen, is that accurate, with what was just read into the record?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And again we see these initials on the right on the top that in the Latinic alphabet appear to be the "T" and the "H," just like the last document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was in the Roman alphabet. Sometimes General Tolimir would write his initials in the Roman alphabet, so I assume these are his initials, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just his initials or also full sentences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, in the Cyrillic script, that letter that appears to be a "T" is a "G", isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct, because the "G" only has the right side and not the left side in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I appreciate that, and I appreciate the education. This document and the writing you see in front of you is only directed to two people, isn't it; and one of those people is General Tolimir, whose initials you've indicated on several occasions during your testimony, and another individual whose initials you haven't been able to indicate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to object to this entire line of questioning. The Prosecutor is not showing the witness the document and the contents of the document, trying to use this witness to state some assertions on account of my client. What I would like to say, that he needs to show the entire contents of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the whole question was whether that's a "T" or a "G," and that's what -- or it was put to the witness that that's a "G," and the witness is saying it's not a "G."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I'm objecting to this other part of the question, where he talks about people included in the contents of this document, not only the interpretation of the signature and all these other things; simply the entire line of this questioning, because I'm asking for the Court's permission to cross-examine this witness. When the document is shown to the witness, I would like him to be shown the contents of the document, whether he's familiar with the document. From this document, you can clearly see that they all refer to the ceasefire in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Big storm in a tea cup. Let the witness see the whole document, unless he's already seen it, and then you proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your request will be considered, if you still maintain it later on, and we'll decide whether it's the case of allowing you to put questions or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that we're right at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My apologies for delaying the proceedings, Your Honours. I had to ask for the witness to stay out of court, because as is apparent, he speaks very good English. I would really like to develop, if I may, not for very long, the observation and objection that Mr. Krgovic raised immediately before the break. We sincerely hope that Your Honour is right and that this is a storm in a tea cup, but sadly we are not sure. We would really like to know where this line of cross-examination is going. We contend that it's not proper for these questions to be asked, that this is an attempt yet again to put more documents into this case which should have been led as part of the Prosecution case. This is not a response to any evidence that General Gvero has led, of course, and therefore that is a consideration that should be at the forefront, we submit, of the Chamber's considerations. Yet again, a witness has been called by another party, and the concentration of the Prosecution effort seems to be directed at our client, at least at the very moment, and of course it raises again the issue that I raised in Your Honour, the learned Presiding Judge's absence, our right to further cross-examine these witnesses, and the difficulty is any further cross-examination, were we to apply for it, would not be and could not be one or two questions; it would need to be a full-blown cross-examination into this area, but that's a distinct and separate matter, which, for my part, I'm happy to examine at a later stage. At this point in time, we would inquire why these questions are being asked, where the Prosecution are going, and what they're hoping to prove by asking these particular questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Why you, Mr. McCloskey, and not Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because it's a policy question, based on quite a bit more than just the witness, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but -- one moment, let me interrupt you. Let's divide it into two parts, because one part is certainly not a policy; he's just asking for Mr. Vanderpuye, what's the general purpose of this line of questions and where he's heading, and then if you want to address the question of whether you are introducing once more documents which you could have dealt with during your case in chief, it's another; and I would need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I also have a problem with Defence counsel asking counsel, in the middle of a cross-examination, where cross-examination is going. It's none of his business. It's his job to figure it out. We always tell them, and we will tell them. That's not a problem, but it's a fascinating question to get, and we will tell him it's not a mystery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we still consider it a storm in a tea cup, in spite of what you've both stated. Our position is a very simple one, Mr. Josse and Mr. McCloskey. Later on, if it's the case of you still -- and when I say "you," it's you, Mr. Krgovic or whoever, still maintaining an interest in cross-examining the witness, we will consider such a request at the right time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could persist for one moment. I don't mean the last witness, the one before that, I objected to a document and was told that I should have objected to the document at the time it was introduced and before the witness had attested to it; and that's what we're doing now. We're trying to stop this off -- head this off at the pass, so to speak. We submit that these questions should not be asked, that this is improper. In fact, I mean, I could develop it further. I was hoping I might get a response from the Prosecution. We say it's outside the scope of the indictment, in fact, if one looks at paragraphs 50 and 51 of the indictment. This is outside the period in relation to humanitarian convoys. We also submit that these documents should have been part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that you have submitted already. And the fact that we have answered you the way we have means that we do not entertain your submission as a valid one in this particular circumstance, so that I think we've made that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So later on you will have every opportunity to cross-examine the witness, if you still do wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And will the Court ever entertain an objection on the basis that a line of questioning is improper, too late, should have happened earlier, falls outside the scope of the indictment? Because if not, we won't make the objection again. I'm not here to waste the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a very compound question. You don't need to, Mr. McCloskey, you don't need to. It's a very compound question which we are not bound to answer, because we've made it clear that we deal with each case as it arises and depending on the circumstances pertaining to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It might be helpful, Mr. President, these materials, we in July went by this Banja Luka archive, which is this thing which has been developing over the years, and whenever we look into it or go by, it has some different or new materials in it. So we found all these Main Staff materials, and we gave them all to the Defence. This was back, I don't know, July/August. They're disclosed on 25 July. So they couldn't have been part of our case. They're the kind of things that come up years and years after the war. They've been provided to everyone. They clearly had Gvero's name on it and others on it, and that's the history of that. And if there's more particular information that you would like us to say, I'm sure Mr. Vanderpuye is better qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I may say, that's very, very helpful to know that. Of course, it illustrates how completely defenceless we were in the situation, bearing in mind this is not our witness and we have, as yet, called no witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely why we've made ourselves clear that at the end of the Prosecution's cross-examination, there is still a request for further cross-examination on your part, we will entertain that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, clearly the Miletic team is taking full advantage, as much as they can, of these documents, and Gvero's name is all over them. So this late -- I don't understand how they've been taken advantage of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, still it's a storm in a tea cup, according to us, so try not to stir it too much, Mr. McCloskey, because it will spill over. So Mr. Vanderpuye, we need to get the witness first, but do you wish to add anything? Okay, that you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, we had some issues to discuss which have got nothing to do with you, obviously, but I would suggest things looking as they are at present, that if you really want to go home for the weekend, that you try to restrict your answers, keep them as short as possible. Otherwise, I'm afraid you'll be here and return to finish your testimony on Tuesday. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you again, sir. If I could have 65 ter 4015 in e-court, please. I'd like to show you this document. All right. This is a letter, and you indicated, I think a little earlier this morning, that some of the documents you prepared or handled in the course of your duties included letters. And you can see this is a letter. If we could go down -- or, rather, to the second page. If we can go down, we can -- 7057 ERN, if we could go to that page. Okay. We can see that this is all signed by Robert Gordon. Are you familiar with that name, first of all, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the type of document that you would handle in your duties back in 1995? And can we go back to the front page, please, so that he can take a look at that. And if we can zoom out so he can see the whole page, that might be helpful. Well, just so the rest of us are aware, this is a -- it's a letter, and it's regarding permission for a helicopter, and it's in relation to the furtherance to the peace plan. I'm not asking you to read the document. I just want to know if it's the type of document that you've seen or handled during your duties in 1995, that's all.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, you can see that this document is directed to Milan Gvero. That's on the left-hand side of the document, right, across from the date where it says "19 January 1995"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the letterhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And the top of this document, you see those initials that we've seen before that in the Latinic script appears to be "PH" which we submit is a "G." You don't recognise those initials, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise any other initials on this document? And let me just direct your attention to what I'm referring to, and that's written right above -- well, if we could just blow up the right-hand side of this screen. Do you recognise any of the initials on the right-hand side where it appears to read "20.01"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get a translation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First I heard the interpreters say that they did not hear the answer. Then I heard the words, "I am not familiar." Was that his answer? I take it that it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, so that clears things for us. You may proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You don't recognise any initials that are indicated above where it's written "20.01"? I just want to make sure that we're clear on that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this document indicates that it's to go to the 1st Krajina Corps by fax, Herzegovina Corps by telegram, that's correct, isn't it, and indicates the date 20th of January, "20.01"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And those initials above "20.01" are General Tolimir's initials, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are his initials, but they pertain to the text above the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, thank you for that. If we could go to 65 ter 4000. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you recognise what kind of document this is, don't you? This is a document that's directed to the UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo, and it relates to the disposition of convoy request; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the contents are quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. And whose signature is that, by the way, on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer that question. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. This document and the last one are not translated. I just want to make sure I'm not missing something on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Obviously, I'm at a severe disadvantage here. Obviously, Mr. Krgovic is able to read the document, and that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand they're being translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They are in the process of being translated. I apologise, I suffer from the same disability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whose signature that is at the bottom, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you, that it's not General Milovanovic's signature. I cannot identify it. Perhaps if you zoom in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we zoom in further, please. And further. It should be sufficient, at least to see whether there is a "za" or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the upper left-hand corner, it says "for," "za," and it looks like Pandzic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask: Colonel Pandzic was authorised to sign on behalf of the Chief of Staff, right? These particular documents, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a certain point in time, where certain documents are concerned, as the duty administrator, since there were no other people around, he sought approval to sign a document, so he was authorised only to sign a particular document, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And if we could go to page -- let me put the date of this document on the record. It's 22 February 1995. And if we could go to page 5 in e-court, please, ERN 7741. That's right. And if we could just blow up the area where the two circles are, written "nee" and "da." All right. And it refers to convoy number 23-297/01, 21 February 1995, and it relates to the delivery of salt to the Sarajevo Airport in accordance with the agreement on snow and ice cleaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, what I want to direct your attention to is immediately -- I should say in between these two circles, you see what appears to be that "TH" again, don't you; in Cyrillic, at least the letter "G"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my mind, this is "Tolimir, Aleksandar," in the Roman alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What is it in the Cyrillic alphabet?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right, it says "why" [Realtime transcript read in error, "Y"] in the Roman alphabet, and this is why I assume it is all in the Roman alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, it is not "Y," in the letter "Y," but "why" as in for what reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's just go to the next page. If we could zoom in again. Thank you. This is ERN 7743, for the record, 774 -- all right, 7743, for the record, then. And if we could blow up the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to direct your attention to the letters immediately below where it's written "nee," followed by an explanation mark. That's the same "TH," isn't it, or the same "G" in Cyrillic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to object to this line of questioning. The letter "T" is the same both in the Roman alphabet and in the Cyrillic alphabet. This is not a handwriting expert. The witness ask can ask him -- the Prosecutor can ask him whether he can recognise the signature, but now to tell us whether something is in the Roman or in the Cyrillic alphabet, I don't think that this is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe not for you, but I think Mr. Josse and Mr. Vanderpuye are in the same position I explained earlier on; they don't read the language, they don't know the language. So I think it is a perfectly legitimate question. We'll see what follows afterwards, but for the time being I think it is a harmless one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, these are the same letter we've seen on all of the documents I've shown you, pretty much, until now, Cyrillic or Latinic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letters are slightly different. To me, it looks like "Tolimir, Aleksandar," in the Roman or Latinic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you explain why you would see "Tolimir, Aleksandar," on a document directing Toso and Gvero to look at a particular item by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tolimir, Aleksandar, was at the command post, the command post of General Gvero's -- General Gvero's command post was several kilometres away, and he was not able to see the documents unless they were sent by mail. We didn't take the documents to Gvero so that he could have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I showed you 65 ter 4010 and 65 ter 4028. All right, let me show you 65 ter 4010. We need to go to page 6842, please. 4010, this is -- okay. Let's just do 4028 instead. Great. And if we could go five pages up to ERN ending 7150. I suppose that would be page 6. This is the document that I showed you earlier, and on this document you identified the -- well, I should say the initials of Zdravko Tolimir on the right-hand side. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And are you telling us that what is written on the top right-hand corner is what you described as "T, Aleksandar"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please be told to read what it says next to the signature, the word that is next, the one that begins with "Tol," T-O-L, on the right-hand side? And if the Prosecutor wants to, perhaps he can ask the witness to check whether this is Gvero's signature or not, so that he stops beating about the bush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Forget about the beating about the bush, but reading, I think, would help everyone. And then I think the suggestion made by Mr. Krgovic, that you try to identify the signature, would also be useful, if you want to do it. Otherwise, they will do it on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will happily do it. I think I've gone over this document with the witness already, which is why I haven't done it. I asked him about the "A/A," I asked him about what was read, and I think my colleague tried to read this into the record. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are correct. This is the one where Ms. Soljan couldn't read the last word, and the witness neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And all I'm asking him at this point is whether or not what is depicted in the top right-hand corner, the "G", at least, in Cyrillic -- that's right -- whether or not that is what he described just recently on the other document as "T," I think he said, "Aleksandar."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that the same to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks similar, but there are some additional lines underneath it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the two documents that I showed you, 4028 and 4010, I believe, those were both documents -- well, this one, as you can see on the right-hand side, you identified General Mladic's initials, and it directs Toso and Gvero to attend to this -- to attend to this matter; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says "Toso and Gvero," that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it would make sense, would it not, that being directed to attend to this matter by General Mladic, that they would attend to that matter, and that would be indicated or consistent with them placing their initials immediately near the direction. You've seen it during your work in 1995. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Two questions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's right. Do you want to split them? Otherwise, if the witness can answer both. The important thing is that he realises that there are two questions in one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you understand the question or would you like me to rephrase, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're going too slow, Mr. Vanderpuye. Rephrase it, please, and split it into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is consistent that officers in the Main Staff, when directed to attend to a matter by General Mladic, as in this context that you've seen, would place their initials on that document to indicate that they have attended to it? You can answer that "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it is true on this document, 4028, that there are only two officers to which this direction is indicated, and that would be Toso and Gvero; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but that doesn't mean that Gvero actually signed it. Somebody could have signed this on his behalf, somebody from his organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be indicated, sir? Wouldn't it say on the document that it's being received or processed or handled by somebody other than the person to whom it's directed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually only the initials were put in of the person that read the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, in fact, on the circle -- above the circle, where it's written "ne e," my colleague will read that to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I fully agree."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You recognise that, right, and you see, immediately following that, those same initials?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that these two initials are different, the one to the left of the United Nations emblem, where it says: "I fully agree," and to the right of those two letters, "A/A," there is a similar sign, and there it says: "Tol." So I assume that the initials that are higher up are General Tolimir's, in the Roman alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 3999 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another document that is directed to the Command -- UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo. It's dated 22nd February 1995, and it's record number 06/17-192, and it also relates to the disposition of convoys. And if we could just go to the next page ending 7722. Here we see on the right-hand side of the screen the word "da" and we see those same initials. We can agree on that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initials are similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The same initials; right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, we can go all the way through this document, and I can show you this over and over again. I won't belabour the point. If we could just go back to the beginning of this document so that we can get -- have the witness identify the signature at the bottom, that would be helpful. Do you recognise that signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have 65 ter 4040 on the record, please -- I mean in e-court. And if we could zoom out just a little bit so we can see the whole thing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document that is dated 21 April 1995, and it also was addressed to the UNPROFOR Command at Sarajevo. And the number on this one is 06/17-361. Similarly, it is a document that refers to the disposition of convoy requests. And if we could just go to -- well, one page over, the ERN ending 8507. And if we could blow it up in the circle. Do you recognise that, the initials that are there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tolimir, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could go three pages forward to the ERN ending 8510.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's written in here, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, this "Tolimir" which you've indicated looks a little bit different than the one you indicated before; right? Should I --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the Roman alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go over to the page ending 8510.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can't find that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fascinating. I don't see it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Josse. Let's check, please. Have we found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it managed not to find its way into e-court. I have a hard copy of it. We can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So just --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I could go to a different page just as easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, go to another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to 8515.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you can see the "da" is written in Cyrillic. The initials next to it, tell us what those are.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again it looks to me to be in the Latinic and that it is Aleksandar Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What is it in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I'd like to show you some other documents, if I could. I'd like to have 4065 in e-court, please. And I have an original of this document that I'd like to show the witness as well. And what we see here is another document that's directed to the Command of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, and I'd like to focus in, if I could, on the signature. First of all, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we put this, please, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have the original of that document before you. Would you like to -- it's on the desk. Would you like to take a look at that? Are you able to make that out, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.
